newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia wants U.N. troops to leave Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatia wants U.N. troops to leave Serb enclave.

text.p: The Croatian government said on Thursday extension of the current United Nations mandate in the last Serb area of Eastern Slavonia would hinder its peaceful reintegration with the rest of the country.

"I claim that the UNTAES (U.N. Transitional Administration of Eastern Slavonia) is beginning to become a hindrance of further reintegration," said the influential Minister for Reconstruction and Development, Jure Radic.

"Because, in order for many parts of the (Croatian) system to be incorporated in Eastern Slavonia, the gates of that region have to be wide open," Radic said during a cabinet session aired on the national television.

The government said it would ask the U.N. Security Council not to extend the military component of the U.N. mandate beyond its current expiry date on July 15, and to start withdrawing some 5,000 U.N. troops immediately afterwards.

The demand is an apparent reaction to recent hints by the United States that it may back the extension of the U.N. military mission in Eastern Slavonia if Zagreb does not permit the return of ethnic Serbs to other parts of Croatia.
The U.S. Secretary of State, Madeleine Albright, told the Croatian leader Franjo Tudjman some two weeks ago that she expected him urgently to improve the treatment of the local Serb population.

Belgrade, which supported the Serb rebellion in Eastern Slavonia and two other enclaves in central Croatia throughout the 1991-95 war, immediately grabbed the opportunity and joined the calls for extension of the mandate till January 15.

Tudjman replied to criticism with two conciliatory speeches, including one delivered in the region's capital Vukovar last Sunday, where he called for reconciliation and forgiveness between Serbs and Croats.
Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic said the "message to the international community is that we fullfilled all the aspects stipulated by the government's letter to the Security Council."

He was referring to the letter in which the government months ago offered the Serb minority in Eastern Slavonia participation in the local administration and police force, temporary suspension of military service and other benefits.
Granic said Zagreb would accept a U.N. civilian monitoring mission, but that the "withdrawal of the military component should start right away".

In support of the demand, ministers cited the fact that many local assemblies elected in the April 13 municipal poll have to meet outside Eastern Slavonia, as the U.N. troops could not guarantee safety to the elected Croatian representatives.
Radic said the government is planning to return some 10,000 Croatian refugees to Vukovar, and 40,000 to the entire region, by the onset of the winter.

Over 80,000 Croats were expelled from the region by Serb extremists in the early stages of the war. The region is currently inhabited by some 150,000 people, one third of whom are refugees from other parts of Croatia.
The government is ready to secure in the next three months the return of some 2,700 Serb families to their homes in other parts of Croatia, Radic said.

Over 150,000 Serbs fled the country in two days of August 1995, fearing retribution from advancing Croatian army troops. Some 10,000 Serbs stayed, and 17,000 have returned since, but they still face occasional harassment and intimidation.

But Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa said the government cannot guarantee the safety of those Serb refugees who return to their homes in government-held territory without its consent and without following the agreed prcedures.
